title: HostedAPI concurrent stream starvation incident diary
content:
Summary:

On 2029-06-14 starting ~03:22 UTC we observed a rapid spike in p95/p99 request latency for the Hosted API streaming endpoint and a concurrent increase in 5xx errors. The symptom set looked like streaming responses stalling mid-session (clients observed long silence), followed by connection resets and an elevated 5xx rate. Impact window lasted ~45 minutes until mitigations took effect.

High level impact:
- Duration: ~03:22 UTC -> ~04:07 UTC peak with tail effects until ~05:10 UTC
- Customer-visible: elevated p95 from ~600ms to ~9s, p99 to ~23s for streaming requests
- Error rate: 5xx rose to ~4% of requests at peak (baseline ~0.02%)
- Affected product: hosted-api streaming (chunked/event-stream style) in us-west-2 primary region
- Severity: P0 (customer-facing outage for streaming flows)

Quick synopsis of what happened (working hypothesis):
A combination of the ephemeral-worker scheduler permitting unbounded concurrency for long-lived streaming sessions plus increased KV-cache eviction pressure created a head-of-line blocking situation. Many streaming sessions retained per-session resources (KV leases, socket workers) while stalled waiting for prefix/KV fetches; the scheduler prioritized newly arriving short-prefetch requests over stalled streams which kept the number of active worker slots saturated. This produced starvation for progress on existing streams, exacerbating latency and creating connection timeouts/5xx.

Timeline (UTC, all times approximate from traces/telemetry):
- 03:20:56 Initial telemetry: small uptick in KV cache misses for prefix group A
- 03:21:40 First client-side reports (Slack #sre-hosted-api): intermittent stream silence
- 03:22:07 p95 starts rising sharply; stream stall alerts fire at 03:22:34
- 03:23:05 5xx rate begins climbing; network-level dashboards show no obvious infra network blips
- 03:24:40 Ops detect worker pool CPU within expected range but ephemeral-worker count saturated
- 03:26:12 Mitigation 1: throttle new streaming session accepts (edge rule) rolled out to 10% of ingress hosts
- 03:29:18 Mitigation 2: temporarily increase ephemeral worker pool soft limit by +20% (config flag)
- 03:34:00 Mitigation 3: route small portion of traffic to standby region (us-east-1) as fallback; observed partial recovery in routed requests
- 03:45:00 Root cause patch candidate prepared (scheduler change to enforce per-session slot cap)
- 03:52:00 Hotfix rollout to canary nodes; metrics show p95 trending down on canary
- 04:07:00 Hotfix promoted cluster-wide; p95 returned close to baseline within ~10m but tail p99 remained elevated for longer as backlog drained

What we saw in the logs (selected snippets):
- "ephemeral-worker: pool saturated, waiting_for_slot=true session_id=..." (hundreds/sec)
- "kv-fetch: miss prefix=A pid=... latency=420ms" repeated and coalescing with "stream-heartbeat: missed"
- "scheduler: allocated slot to short-lifetime-request session_id=.. priority=high"

Root cause analysis (evidence-backed):
- Immediate proximate cause: scheduler policy allowed a high number of concurrent streaming sessions to hold ephemeral slots while blocking on KV fetches; there was no robust fairness enforcement between long-lived streaming sessions and short-lived inference calls.
- Contributing factor: recent KV cache policy change (rolled 2029-06-10) reduced cache retention for some prefix groups under memory pressure; this led to transient increases in KV fetch latency and cache miss amplification.
- Additional factor: adaptive batcher heuristics (deployed 2029-05-30) increased short-request burst concurrency which consumed spare worker slots and prevented starved streaming sessions from getting CPU time.
- System limits: we had soft caps but they were permissively high and not enforced for long-lived sessions. Circuit-breakers for long-running streaming sessions were incomplete.

Why the mitigations worked:
- Throttling new session accepts reduced ingress of short-lived requests that were consuming scheduler slots, allowing the runtime to prioritize backlog drainage of existing streams.
- Increasing ephemeral worker pool provided immediate headroom while the scheduler fix was prepared.
- Routing to standby region shifted load and reduced pressure on the primary region caches.

Immediate actions taken (ordered):
- Disable adaptive batcher short-request burst path (rollback flag) — executed 03:28 UTC — owner: Lina H.
- Edge throttle for new streaming connections to 60% of normal rate — 03:26 UTC — owner: Diego R.
- Hotfix: scheduler enforces per-session active-slot limit of 2 and fairness queuing for streams — canary 03:52, prod 04:07 — owner: Omar S.

Corrective actions and follow-ups (short/medium/long):
Short (next 72 hours):
- CA-1: Back out adaptive batcher config change and add canary test for burst behavior (owner: Lina H, due: 2029-06-17)
- CA-2: Add SLO-based automatic throttle rule tied to streaming p95 spike (owner: Diego R, due: 2029-06-18)
- CA-3: Post-incident telemetry export and replay of traces for impacted time window (owner: Aisha P, due: 2029-06-17)

Medium (2–6 weeks):
- CA-4: Implement a scheduler fairness algorithm that differentiates long-lived streaming sessions from short RPCs; write unit/integration tests for fairness (owner: Platform Eng, due: 2029-07-01)
- CA-5: KV cache policy revert review and more conservative eviction thresholds; introduce per-prefix telemetry (owner: Applied ML infra, due: 2029-07-05)
- CA-6: Add circuit-breaker and soft eviction for stalled streaming sessions that free ephemeral resources after inactivity threshold (owner: Serving Runtime, due: 2029-07-08)

Long (quarterly roadmap):
- CA-7: Capacity model overhaul to include long-tail streaming occupancy in autoscaling calculations (owner: Infra Capacity, due: 2029-09-30)
- CA-8: Revisit adaptive batching heuristics and add workload-aware canary harness for real traffic patterns (owner: Optimize team, due: 2029-09-30)

Runbook draft (for SRE on-call steps) — put into playbook as an interim v0.1:
1) Detection: alerts are p95 streaming > 2s for 2m or 5xx rate > 1% sustained 5m.
2) Triage: check ephemeral-worker saturation, KV cache miss rate per-prefix, and scheduler queue lengths.
3) Mitigate quickly: apply edge throttle for new streaming sessions (edge flag), disable adaptive burst path, scale ephemeral-worker pool by +20% if safe.
4) If no recovery in 10m: redirect 10-30% of streaming traffic to standby region; coordinate with traffic-shift runbook.
5) Prepare hotfix: deploy scheduler fairness change to canary; monitor p95 trend for canary before cluster roll.
6) Communication: post status updates every 10 minutes to #sre-hosted-api and update incident bridge notes.

Monitoring and alerting changes to make (owners assigned):
- Add per-prefix KV miss ratio panels and alert when miss-rate doubles baseline for >5m (owner: Observability, due: 2029-06-21).
- Add a derived metric: fraction_of_slots_held_by_streams with 1,5,15m windows and alert when >60% sustained (owner: SRE, due: 2029-06-21).
- Create synthetic streaming checks that exercise long-lived session progression (owner: Devexp, due: 2029-06-28).

Open questions / uncertainties:
- Was any particular customer or prefix responsible for a disproportionate portion of the pressure? Traces point to prefix-group A but we need matching client lists. (Action: Aisha to correlate logs -> due 2029-06-17)
- Did the KV cache change indirectly expose a latent bug in the scheduler fairness path, or would the same have happened without the KV change? (Action: post-incident replay and AB test)
- What is the acceptable backoff pattern for streaming sessions vs short requests under SLO tradeoffs? Need product + SRE alignment.

Post-incident communications plan:
- Internal synthesis: SRE summary in #sre-hosted-api and all-hands summary in Eng-ops weekly (owner: Aisha, due: 2029-06-17)
- Customer communications: CS to notify top affected accounts with a short remediation summary and timeline (owner: CS lead, due: 2029-06-18)

Appendix: useful snippets and commands used during the incident:
- Check ephemeral worker saturation: kubectl top pods -l app=ephemeral-worker -n hostedapi-prod | sort -k2
- Sample query for slot-occupancy from metrics backend: sum(rate(slot_held_total{job="ephemeral-worker"}[1m])) by (session_type) / sum(machine_slots)
- Hotfix PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/8212 (scheduler fairness change, includes tests)

Notes to self / informal: this one felt like a classic resource starvation but created by recent config churn + missing fairness. We need tighter pre-rollout canaries for infra-config that affects memory/cache and a lightweight chaos test that simulates a mix of streaming+short requests to detect schedule inversion. Also, make the runbook steps less ad-hoc: keep an 'emergency throttle' flag that can be toggled by on-call without code deploy.

Owners and next steps summary:
- Aisha Patel (SRE lead): coordinate telemetry replay, write incident summary, follow up with CS (due 2029-06-17)
- Lina Huang (Runtime): revert adaptive-batcher burst config, add canary tests (due 2029-06-17)
- Diego Ramirez (Edge/SRE): implement p95-triggered automatic throttle and update playbook (due 2029-06-18)
- Omar Singh (Platform Eng): scheduler fairness immediate patch verification and formal spec (due 2029-07-01)

Status: draft postmortem / runbook addendum. Need more trace correlation and owner sign-offs before marking final.

End of diary.
